newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yen yield curve may steepen if bank worries fade.
newsitem.headline: Yen yield curve may steepen if bank worries fade.

text.p: The yield curve for Japanese interest rates may steepen in the near term if the bond market shifts its focus from fears about Japan's financial system to lower demand and rising supply of long-term bonds, traders said on Friday.

"Since the short end of the yield curve is likely to remain fixed at the current rock-bottom levels, whether the curve steepens or not depends on market sentiment toward the long end of the JGB market," said Kazuhiko Sano, chief strategist at Sumitomo Capital Securities.

Traders said the recent bullishness in Japanese government bonds (JGBs) was mainly led by fears of further falls in land prices and of a further credit crunch at Japanese financial institutions, both related to Japan's bad loan problems.

Without such worries to prop them up, they said, JGBs would be vulnerable to declines based on supply-demand factors, as the Bank of Japan (BOJ) halved the volume of its long-term JGB buying this year and the supply of long-term yen bonds is expected to increase.
"The fact that JGBs rallied on such unrealistic (financial) fears suggests the rally has entered its last stage," said Takuma Hayakawa, manager of bond trading at LTCB Securities.
On Thursday, JGB yields jumped when fears about the financial system were salved by reports that Japan is considering using public funds to buy land held as collateral by troubled financial firms.
The key 182nd 10-year JGB yield rose by 0.075 to 2.445 percent at Thursday's finish, compared with a record-low 2.330 percent hit in December last year.

Although this suggests the central bank may no longer be eager to check a rise in long-term JGB yields, most market participants believe the BOJ will not raise interest rates before the end of this year, if then, traders said.
Japan's economic recovery this year is expected to be anaemic due to fiscal tightening from April 1.
But some traders said a hint of caution on inflation on Wednesday by BOJ governor Yasuo Matsushita might suggest the bank is preparing for higher interest rates.

Although Matsushita said that domestic prices did not show signs of moving into an upward trend, he also said the weak yen had "speeded up the tempo of the rise in prices of imports and we need to carefully watch domestic prices from now on".

A senior dealer at one of Japan's big four brokerages said the market believes there will be no change in the interest rate outlook in the near future, but if the yield curve were to steepen, it would do so because of inflation fears or oversupply.

"Using public funds (to solve Japan's bad loan problems) means the government would have to raise funds through the markets, perhaps by issuing municipal bonds, and many participants have not yet realised this," he said.
Additional supply pressures may come from borrowers' preference for issuing longer-term bonds on the belief that the recent downtrend in long-term yields may continue, he said.

This week triple-A-rated Chubu Electric Power Co launched 30 billion yen worth of 3.25 percent 20-year straight bonds. The coupon was set even lower than the 3.30 percent for 20-year bonds launched on February 5 by East Japan Railway, which is also rated triple A.
A spokesman at Chubu said the company chose a 20-year maturity because the market seemed buoyant enough to absorb the very long-term bond.
